questions.q: What specific cost does point-to-point integration carry that doesn't show up on day one?
options: Point-to-point connections are always slower than middleware-based connections
Every new system needing to talk to Salesforce needs its own bespoke connection, and the number of connections grows roughly with the square of the number of systems involved
Point-to-point connections cannot use Named Credentials
Point-to-point connections are illegal under Salesforce's terms of service
questions.explain: As more systems connect point-to-point, the number of bespoke connections (and the maintenance burden of each one potentially breaking the others) grows disproportionately, which is the real, delayed cost of this approach.

questions.q: What does a middleware hub change about how systems connect to Salesforce, compared to point-to-point integration?
options: Each system connects once to the hub, which handles translation, routing, and orchestration between all connected systems
A middleware hub eliminates the need for any authentication between systems
A middleware hub only works for batch integrations, never real-time ones
A middleware hub requires removing all existing point-to-point connections immediately
questions.explain: The hub model's core benefit is that each system only needs one connection -- to the hub -- rather than a separate bespoke connection to every other system it needs to reach.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say Doverfield's identity-provider integration (Lesson 3) and customer-portal integration (Lesson 4) should have been considered together, in hindsight?
options: Because they use the exact same Apex code

Because both touch the same underlying question -- who is allowed to authenticate as what kind of user -- and building them as unrelated, sequential efforts baked in assumptions the later one had to work around
Because customer portals always require a separate identity provider by law
Because Lesson 3 and Lesson 4 use the same External ID field
questions.explain: Sequencing matters: because the two integrations address closely related identity questions, building them independently and sequentially left the portal work needing to retrofit around decisions the SSO work had already made.

questions.q: What does treating Platform Events and Change Data Capture as 'one shared event backbone' mean in this lesson?
options: Using exactly one Platform Event definition for the entire org, regardless of use case

A single place where a business event gets published once, with any number of independent subscribers (ERP sync, warehouse sync, future systems) listening to that same stream, rather than each building its own bespoke pipeline
Disabling Change Data Capture in favor of Platform Events exclusively
Routing every event through the ERP system before it reaches any other subscriber
questions.explain: The point of a shared backbone is that each new subscriber just listens to the existing stream, instead of every integration independently building its own bespoke event-consumption pipeline from scratch.

questions.q: What is the realistic migration approach this lesson recommends for moving Doverfield's existing point-to-point connections onto a middleware hub?
options: Ripping out all existing point-to-point connections overnight and rebuilding everything on the hub at once
Routing new integrations through the hub going forward, while migrating the highest-maintenance existing connections onto it over time
Never migrating existing connections, since point-to-point integration has no real downsides
Deleting the ERP integration entirely rather than migrating it
questions.explain: The lesson recommends an incremental approach: new work goes through the hub immediately, and the costliest existing connections get migrated over time, rather than an all-at-once rebuild.
